# Draft:Altab Ali & the Battle of Brick Lane

----
Altab Ali & the Battle of Brick Lane is a 2020 British animated short documentary film surrounds the racist killing of Altab Ali, a young Bangladeshi worker in east London in May of 1978. The film is directed by Diwas Bisht and produced by Dr Emily Keightley and Kazi Ruksana Begum. It tells the tale of the widespread racism faced by the Bangladeshi community living in east London at the time and how the incident inspired a generation of Bangladeshis to join hands in the fight against the racist forces. Using interviews of the activists involved in the anti-racist struggle and striking contrasting imagery, the film tells the tale of the event that marks a turning point in London's race relations.
Production
The film was made in partnership with Loughborough University's Migrant Memory and the Post-colonial Imagination project and the London Borough of Tower Hamlets and was directed by Diwas Bisht, whose background combines visual art, animation, and academic research. The film was a collaboration of young animators who were inspired to share Altab's story. The team behind the film were involved in researching the story through local archives, heritage walks and discussions with people connected to anti-racist activism in East London. The community-based production separates the film from conventional broadcast documentaries and links it to participatory and arts-based research practices.
Synopsis
The film covers the racial attack and killing of Altab Ali as well as the conditions surrounding it in late-1970s East London. It explores the hostility and violence experienced by the Bangladeshi community in the area of Brick Lane and presents the ways in which Ali’s death became a catalyst for resistance. Rather than focusing only on a single act of violence the film broadens its frame to depict the social atmosphere in which racial violence had become part of everyday life for local residents. The film utilises interviews with activists who were involved in the anti-racist struggle alongside strongly contrasting visual imagery. This combination allows the film to move between testimony, historical reconstruction as well as symbolic visualisation. Ultimately, the film is a retelling of an event that marked a turning point in London’s race relations. The structure of the film allows for personal memories and collective political history to be presented together, leading to the film emphasising not only loss and violence but also protest, solidarity, and community self-organisation. Although the film is short, its narrative scope is more than just a biographical memorial. It places Ali’s murder within the larger story of British Bangladeshi settlement, radicalisation, and political awakening. The documentary’s interest lies not only in what happened in 1978, but also how that historic event has been remembered, narrated and passed on. In doing so, it links the anti-racist organising of the late 1970s to later questions of diaspora, identity, and intergenerational memory.
Release and Exhibition
The film was released online on the 4th May 2020, which was the anniversary of Altab Ali’s murder. The launch was an online screening event, the screening was followed by online discussion and Q&A with those involved in making the film. The film was later screened on 24 July 2020 as part of South Asian Heritage Month, once again in an online format. In October 2020, it was listed in the line-up of the North Dakota Human Rights Film Festival, where it appeared among similar films also addressing racism, equality, and social justice. The film had also appeared in academic and public events linked to memory studies; a screening by Bisht under the title “Altab Ali and the Battle of Brick Lane: Unravelling Critical Histories of Anti-Racism of the British Bengali Diaspora Through Participatory Art Methodologies.” These exhibitions place the film in overlapping circuits of public history, university research, activist commemoration and human-rights film culture. The film has continued to circulate online through official and partner channels on websites like YouTube. Its digital circulation formed part of its public function, extending its use beyond festival exhibition into teaching, commemoration, and community heritage work.
Themes, Style and their Significance
One of the film’s major features is its use of animation to address historical violence and community memory. Bisht’s later scholarship on British Bangladeshi memory situates the project exists within a larger effort to explore how “hidden” histories of colonialism, migration, settlement, and postcolonial identity are transmitted across generations". A chapter in his book 'Animating British Bangladeshi Memory' is devoted specifically to the film and is titled “Altab Ali and the Battle of Brick Lane: Animating Multidirectional Memories of the Bangladeshi Anti-Racist Resistance.” Those sources suggest that the film should be understood not only as a documentary about a past event, but also as part of a broader inquiry into memory, diaspora as well as anti-racist cultural work. The film also belongs to a strand of contemporary documentary-making that combines oral testimony with stylised visual artistic interpretation. Official descriptions emphasise interviews, archival research and youth-led historical engagement. As well as this, the project's context places the work within community memory practices rather than mainstream commercial film production. Its stop-motion and illustrated aesthetic help visualise a past that survives in fragments, recollection and public commemoration rather than in a single authoritative archive. In that respect, the film aligns itself with a much wider body of work that uses animation to render historical trauma, silenced histories, and inherited memory in forms that are both accessible and interpretive. Another major theme is the relationship between a place and political memory. The Brick Lane area, Whitechapel, and the later memorialisation of Altab Ali in the urban landscape are central to how this story is told publicly. Ali’s murder is connected to the making of East London as a site of anti-racist struggle. By focusing on that geography, the film presents history not as an abstract national narrative, but as something embedded in streets, memorial sites, marches and neighbourhoods.
Legacy and Impact
The impact of Altab Ali and the Battle of Brick Lane lies in its contribution to the public remembrance of Altab Ali and the anti-racist organisation that followed his murder. Histories of British Bangladeshis and East London anti-racism describe Ali’s death as a key moment in community mobilisation, whilst public memorial culture in the area continues to keep that history physically visible. The film participates within this memorial tradition but does so in a way shaped by animation, oral history as well as collaborative research. Instead of functioning only as a commemorative object, it also functions as a tool for education and intergenerational transmission. The project’s educational impact is especially evident in its connection to The Fight for Equality, a resource developed with young people from George Green School to teach local anti-racist history. On the Tower Hamlets project page, the film appears alongside that educational resource, suggesting that it was conceived not only as a standalone short film but as a part of a larger attempt to preserve and circulate the radical history of East London. In this context, the film presents how documentary and animation can function simultaneously as research output, public history, community memory work, and anti-racist pedagogy.
Visual Inspiration
The film’s visual inspirations drew on archival and documentary materials connected to anti-racist activism in East London. Coverage of exhibitions and public-history projects linked to the Altab Ali story has highlighted photographs by Paul Trevor, Syd Shelton, and Tom Learmonth, whose images documented protest, procession, and community resistance around Brick Lane in the late 1970s. The photographers were credited within the film as the inspiration for the animation, further emphasising the link animation has to communicating memory and history.
Reception
Published critical reception appears to have been limited, most coverage came from institutional, community, and project-based platforms rather than from mainstream film critics. The film’s public life was therefore shaped less by conventional review culture, and more by commemorative, educational and activist culture.
Music
The film does not prominently include  music until the credits, as to create more of a focus on the oral-history testimonies. However the music is credited as including Dangerous Games by Terry Divine-King, Gossamer Lines 2 by Noah Sorota.
Marketing and Promotion
The film was promoted mainly through community, educational and festival channels rather than through commercial marketing campaigns. Partner organisation's including the London Borough of Tower Hamlets and Loughborough University’s Migrant Memories and the Post-colonial Imagination project publicised the film through dedicated web pages that featured a trailer, production stills, and descriptions of its historical and educational aims. Promotional material described the film as an animated documentary intended to keep alive the history of anti-racist struggle in East London and to support the wider Fight for Equality. After its online launch, the film continued to be promoted through public-event and heritage platforms. It was advertised for an online screening during South Asian Heritage Month in 2020, it would also circulate through film festivals and private screenings. The film’s promotion was closely tied to public history, education, and festival exhibition rather than to mainstream theatrical advertising.
